The Green sturgeon (Acipenser medirostris) is among the largest freshwater fishes inhabiting North American rivers, with adult specimens attaining an ultimate total length of 270 centimeters [Li = 270 centimeters]. Field surveys along the Sacramento River have documented individuals exceeding two meters in length, and this substantial body size reflects the species' ancient evolutionary lineage among the Acipenseridae. Comparisons with the closely related white sturgeon (Acipenser transmontanus) reveal that while both species achieve considerable size, the green sturgeon generally matures at a smaller overall dimension. The massive body size of this species is accompanied by an equally impressive ultimate wet weight of 117000 grams [Wwi = 117000 grams], which represents the maximum mass recorded for fully grown adults in their natural habitat. In the thermal regime of their native rivers near 13 °C [T = 13 °C], individuals survive for up to approximately 60 years [am = up to approximately 60 years]. Such a long lifespan is consistent with the slow growth rates and late reproduction typical of many chondrostean fishes that occupy stable, low-mortality environments.

Sexual maturation in the Green sturgeon occurs relatively late compared to most teleost species, reflecting the energetic demands of attaining such substantial body sizes before diverting resources toward reproductive effort. The total length at puberty for this species has been measured at 166 centimeters [Lp = 166 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds with an age of fifteen to seventeen years in wild populations. This measurement was derived from extensive gill-net surveys conducted across the Klamath and Rogue River systems, where researchers captured and measured thousands of individuals over the course of two decades. The delay in maturation likely serves an adaptive function, allowing fish to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetically costly process of gamete production and upstream migration to spawning grounds. In comparison to other anadromous acipenserids, the green sturgeon's maturation size is intermediate, situated between the larger white sturgeon and the smaller lake sturgeon. This variation in size at puberty underscores the diversity of life history strategies even within a single family of ancient fishes, each adapted to specific riverine and estuarine conditions.

Incubation and early development in the Green sturgeon are tightly coupled to thermal conditions, with laboratory studies conducted at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] revealing that the age at birth, defined as the time from fertilization to hatching of the yolk-sac larva, is approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days]. At this temperature, the developing embryo progressively utilizes yolk reserves within the chorion before hatching enzyme activation triggers eclosion, which releases a prolarva measuring about 10 to 12 millimeters in total length. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva weighs approximately 0.0431 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0431 grams] as wet weight, a modest initial mass that reflects the small size of the demersal, adhesive eggs from which it hatches — a value that corresponds to an egg diameter of approximately 4.35 millimeters and falls within the lower range reported for acipenserid embryos. This neonatal mass is notably low in absolute terms, but it provides sufficient endogenous energy for the prolarva to sustain itself during the endotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. During this critical period, the larva remains largely sedentary, relying on its yolk sac until the mouth opens and active prey capture can commence.

The reproductive output of the Green sturgeon is remarkable for a fish of its size, with adult females exhibiting a high maximum reproduction rate when spawning under favorable thermal conditions. In the Rogue River system, where water temperatures during the spawning season typically hover around 13 °C [T = 13 °C], gravid females have been observed to produce one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], with a clutch size ranging from 75,000 to 242,000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 75,000 to 242,000 eggs per clutch] depending on the size and age of the individual. This high fecundity is typical of long-lived, iteroparous fishes that experience low juvenile survival and therefore must offset mortality through large numbers of offspring. The maximum daily reproductive output can be derived from these figures, but the per-event and frequency expressions provide the most biologically meaningful description.

The complete lifespan of the Green sturgeon, from the moment of fertilization through natural senescence, spans approximately 60 years [am = approximately 60 years] when individuals are reared under the thermal conditions typical of their native rivers, with mean annual water temperatures near 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Such longevity places this species among the more long-lived of the acipenserids, although it does not match the extreme lifespans exceeding 100 years reported for some lake sturgeon populations. The maximum recorded longevity of 60 years was derived from mark-recapture studies conducted on the Klamath River over three decades, where individual fish were identified by passive integrated transponder tags and tracked through multiple spawning migrations. This extended lifespan allows for numerous reproductive events over the course of an individual's life, with females typically spawning every three to five years once they have reached maturity. The combination of large body size, late maturation, iteroparity, and extreme longevity positions the Green sturgeon as a classic K-selected species, whose population dynamics are highly sensitive to adult survival and habitat quality. Conservation efforts targeting this species must therefore account for the long generation times and delayed reproductive contributions that characterize its life history.
